The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) have all said repeatedly that the Canadian banking system is sound. subsubtopic: NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S FUND RAISING MAIL CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the House a matter which is most disturbing. Yesterday I received, as thousands of Canadians have been receiving through the regular mail, a business envelope with the words "Taxation Notice; avis d'impots" in bold, red print in the upper left-hand corner. Through the cellophane window of the business envelope Canadians see their name and address, postal code, and a number preceded by the letters "TX".
Clearly anyone seeing such an envelope would be led to believe that some level of Government was writing to them with regard to taxes assessed or owing.

November 1, 1985

Mr. Speaker, does one get a tax assessment notice or a reminder when opening the envelope? Or does one get an official Government document? No, Mr. Speaker, one gets a picture of the Leader of the New Democratic Party and a letter asking for a financial contribution to the NDP.

This technique is one which is a misrepresentation, at best. It misleads Canadians into thinking their municipality or federal Government is corresponding with them when, really, it is only an NDP ploy for money.
Canadians will not appreciate this joke being played on them. They will find this brand of NDP humour to be in bad taste. All Canadians who are victimized by this NDP brainstorm should demonstrate their disgust by throwing this so-called "taxation notice" in the garbage.
The only good thing which can be said about this trick is that the NDP has finally admitted that it, its policies and its tactics, are taxing to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF FORT GARRY WOMEN'S RESOURCE CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time women's centres across the country have been experiencing severe financial problems due to federal funding cut-backs.
The Fort Garry Women's Resource Centre in Winnipeg is but one example. This centre provides an invaluable service to many Manitoban women, offering information and referral services, crisis intervention, counselling and volunteer training, to name only a few of its services. Much is done at these centres, and it is done at a very low cost and in an efficient manner.
Ongoing funding must occur, and once again the Manitoba Government is stepping in to replace vanishing federal funds. The Manitoba Government is willing to offer $21,000 in core funding, which is in addition to the $24,000 offered by the province for programming moneys.
We are asking the federal Government to be prepared to match that amount, knowing full well that, without core funding, programs are difficult to deliver, with no place to deliver them from and no staff to provide the services.
Given the promises of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), not only during the election campaign but during the televised debates, to offer money for such centres, will the Government finally deliver on the many promises made to Canadian women, starting with the Fort Garry Women's Resource Centre?

Mr. Speaker, I have a very serious question for the Minister of the Environment. Action is finally being taken on the Niagara River, but an even more dangerous situation is becoming apparent on the St. Clair River. speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can certainly confirm that a tar-like slick has been found in the St. Clair River as recently as this fall, in addition to the slicks which were found earlier, I believe in August of 1984. It is clear that the substances do contain chlorinated hydrocarbons, including the cancer-causing agent, dioxin.
As soon as I found out about the most recent discovery 1 mobilized the top experts in the country, including those within my Department, but not excluding outside experts, for the purpose of confirming the preliminary findings and advising on the potential source.
Briefly, there are two possibilities; first, a direct discharge into the river from industries along the river; second, the possibility of a seepage from underneath the river bed from dump sites which are 30 or 40 years old. I will advise the Hon. Member when the analysis has been completed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (President of the Privy Council) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-45, an Act respecting employment and employer and employee relations in the Senate and House of Commons, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today to begin the second reading debate of Bill C-45. This Bill is a progressive step towards reforming the labour relations process on Parliament Hill. It is based on legislation which was first proposed by the Standing Committee on Management and Members Services and which was unanimously supported by all three political Parties. It is a major step along the road to parliamentary reform and creates for the first time a modern and responsible statutory framework within which a positive approach to labour management relations can be achieved.
Given the subject matter of the Bill, I think it only appropriate that I begin my remarks by acknowledging the tremendous contribution of all parliamentary employees. It is their professionalism and dedication that makes this institution function. Each employee, whether he or she is employed in the House of Commons, the Senate or the Library of Parliament plays a unique and vital role in the effective operation of our institution.

Too often, Mr. Speaker, we forget how lucky we are to be able to rely on such qualified and professional staff to help us in our work. On behalf of Hon. Members on both sides of the House I want to assure parliamentary employees that their efforts do not go unnoticed and are greatly appreciated by all Members of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons has grown rapidly in the past several years. It is now a large and complex organization which employs over 3,000 persons. Unfortunately the evolution and growth of this institution has not been paralleled by the creation of a modern system of labour relations. As a result parliamentary employees do not enjoy the benefits of a contemporary labour relations regime tailored to the special circumstances of Parliament. This Bill will resolve that problem in a progressive and comprehensive fashion.
Because there appears to be some genuine confusion and misunderstanding about the nature of rights presently enjoyed by parliamentary employees, it may be useful to review the history of the collective bargaining debate on the Hill. It is that history which provides the context for the action which we are embarking on today.
The subject of collective bargaining rights for the employees of Parliament has been under discussion for some considerable period of time. In the formal sense the subject was first considered in 1967 by the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Employer and Employee Relations in the Public Service during that committee's deliberations on Bill C-170, namely the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
In its report of February 3, 1967 the committee stated, and I quote:
Your Committee recommends that consideration be given to the introduction of legislation to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act and the Library
November 1, 1985

of Parliament Act to extend to the employees thereunder advantages and rights similar to those provided public servants under Bill C-170.
Unfortunately, no further action was taken with respect to this recommendation.
On a number of occasions since 1967 private Members have tabled Bills which would have provided a legislative framework for collective bargaining by parliamentary employees and questions have also been raised on the floor of the House of Commons. One such question prompted the undertaking of a study on this matter in 1982. This report, known as the Weir Report, after its author Mr. Robert Weir, was tabled in the House in February of 1983. The report analysed the issue and outlined a number of options but made no recommendations. The Weir Report was referred to the Standing Committee on Management and Members Services for further study on February of the same year and, in late 1983, this committee, with the assistance of the Privy Council Office, developed draft legislation on this subject. Events leading up to the election in 1984, and the change of Government which resulted, precluded immediate action on this Bill.
1 must indicate at this time that the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who was my predecessor in this particular capacity, during the summer of 1984 issued a press release in which he indicated the intention of the Liberal Government of the day to proceed with legislation with respect to allowing parliamentary employees the right of collective bargaining, which was in a similar vein to the recommendations which were made to that committee.
The Bill before the House today closely reflects the all-Party consensus which was reflected in the draft legislation that I referred to in 1983. Beginning in the fall of 1983 unions seeking certification as bargaining agents for parliamentary employees filed a series of applications pursuant to the Canada Labour Code. The Canada Labour Code governs labour relations in those areas of the commercial and business world which are subject to the jurisdiction of Parliament, but it does not apply to the Public Service.
There are clearly differences of opinion as to the jurisdiction of the Canada Labour Relations Board in this dispute. The legality of the question has not yet been determined to the satisfaction of all concerned and, because of the way in which legal proceedings have a way of carrying on, it could take months indeed, if not many years, for the element of uncertainty which surrounds this question to be cleared up through the judicial process.

In the end, after lengthy and costly legal proceedings, it is conceivable that, owing to the particular situation of Parliament, parliamentary employes be considered as having no rights, that is without the right to join a union, establish a certified association, or bargain collectively.
In the Government's view, Mr. Speaker, such a situation would be unsatisfactory. Parliamentary employees ought to have the right to bargain collectively and be able to resort to a progressive labour relations system.
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act [English]
Bill C-45 clears away all the jurisdictional doubts which presently exist with respect to the matter by proceeding quickly with a reasoned and reasonable approach to labour relations. It states clearly and unequivocally that parliamentary employees do have the right to organize and bargain collectively. The Bill introduces a comprehensive modern structure for the resolution of labour-management relations on Parliament Hill.
Bill C-45 has three principal aspects. First, it provides a collective bargaining framework for parliamentary employees which is similar to that contained in the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Second, it makes Part III of the Canada Labour Code applicable to parliamentary employees whether or not they are organized. Part III regulates labour standards, including such items as vacations and hours of work. Finally, the Bill makes Part IV of the Canada Labour Code applicable to all employees. Part IV regulates such items as occupational and safety standards.
As indicated, the Bill itself is based very closely on the Public Service Staff Relations Act. The logic of this parallelism is readily apparent. Notwithstanding the special place that Parliament occupies in our governmental system, the role of parliamentary employees is very similar to that of public servants generally.
It is our view that the labour relations framework which governs the Public Service commends itself very strongly to the parliamentary scene because of this fact. The Bill provides that, with specific exceptions, parliamentary employees are entitled to organize and bargain collectively. Exceptions are provided with respect to persons in a managerial or confidential capacity. Persons employed in the offices of Members of Parliament and caucus research groups will not have access to the bargaining provisions provided for in Part I.

I reiterate the fact that this legislation is a matter of some substantial accomplishment in making progress from the original proposal. Parts III and IV of the Canada Labour Code will be made applicable to all parliamentary employees regardless of whether or not they are organized. In this way, minimum protection with respect to working conditions and labour standards will be available to all who work on our behalf in this place and on the precincts of Parliament Hill.
Part I of the Bill closely resembles the Public Service Staff Relations Act which at present governs labour relations in the Public Service. The Public Service Staff Relations Board is established as the advisory board to administer this legislation.

Now is the time to bring forward true reform with respect to labour relations on Parliament Hill. Although I can see that Bill C-45 is a start, it surely requires, in my view, a step which we must take unanimously. This legislation will mean the end to an era of unilateral decisions in matters of employee-employer relations for most employees of Parliament. It establishes a system whereby Parliament and its employees will jointly determine the terms and conditions of employment in collective bargaining. We have in Canada a good log-book of experience in employee-employer relations. At the federal level we have, as I said, accumulated 20 years of experience with the Public Service Staff Relations Act. We should be able to build upon this strong background. Both parties, in my view, the employee and the employer, should adapt quickly to their new relationship. We should not have to go through the growing pains we did in
1967. I am sure that with good will and patience, numerous benefits will come to both sides.
One can justifiably ask why we do not make the Canada Labour Code applicable to employees of Parliament rather than an Act which draws inspiration itself from the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the Canada Labour Code. While substantial differences exist between the two labour relations statutes, it is believed by some-and I take it this is going to be debated in committee-that there is good and sufficient reason to adopt special legislation with particular characteristics to accommodate Parliament with its complexities and necessities such as the maintenance of essential services. Of course, some people would wonder how one could say that Parliament is an essential service. I would take it that some people at some time would rather not have us here debating and would say that we are not that essential. 1 would like to address a few problems pertaining to this Bill which I feel needs discussion and change.

As you know, Mr. Speaker, it is the Public Service Employment Act which governs hiring practices and methods based on the merit system, that is, any nomination must be based on merit. More specifically, Section 10 of the Public Service Employment Act states:

Mr. Speaker, another weakness of this document is the issue of job classification and job classification standards.
In a report to Parliament by the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations, we examined the entire subject of classification. I would ask Hon. Members to refer to the document on page 4720 for the explanatory text on classification, which reads, for instance, and I quote:

Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act is another point. There is the matter of arbitration as well. We will certainly comment on all those points and we hope our contribution will bring the required clarifications to the Bill.
Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that special legislation be adopted to govern labour relations in Parliament is a compromise between two extreme positions, namely that it is a question of parliamentary privilege. It is the kind of argument which has often been used here. We used to be told: Of course, parliamentary privilege eliminates any possibility for Parliament Hill employees to become unionized. There has been a certain evolution over the past few years, so that thanks to the Constitution and the unions' persistence before the Staff Relations Board, Parliament is finally starting to move and doing something which I feel is both constructive and necessary.
Designated employees of Parliament will be divided into three categories: House of Commons, Senate, Library of Parliament.
The employees hired by Hon. Members and working for them in their offices will not be subject to collective bargaining, although they will be covered, as all parliamentary employees, by Parts III and IV of the Canada Lobour Code which govern their terms and conditions of employment. There are also provisions governing occupational safety and health which apply to all employees working on Parliament Hill.
Bill C-45 will determine every aspect of the staff relations system which will apply only to employees working on Parliament Hill for the Senate, the House of Commons, and the Library of Parliament. As stated in this legislation, some of these employees will be designated employees.
According to the General Provisions of the Canada Labour Code, the right to collective bargaining stems only from legislation. Until now, no collective bargaining legislation had applied to Parliament. Parliament employees could not benefit from the Public Service Staff Relations Act because they did not belong to the Public Service and were not subject to the Canada Labour Code because of the privilege of Parliament to which I referred earlier.
Part I of Bill C-45 indicates that certain categories of parliamentary employees could join a union to protect their rights and set up a legal structure for collective bargaining and grievance procedure.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-45 is to create a framework very similar to that applicable to all Public Service employees, with a number of restrictions in line with those currently in force in the private sector.
The Canada Labour Code generally recognizes the right of workers to organize for the purpose of bargaining collectively their working conditions. The law creates a structure within which this agreement is made and which is administered by a labour relations board. As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the fact that you have a constitutional right does not necessarily make

November 1, 1985
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act the issue any clearer. The constitutional right is there, but in most jurisdictions, there is a law to define it.
The law creates a structure within which this agreement takes place and which is administered by a board. Employees in the groups judged apt to collective bargaining, or bargaining units, then choose their union representatives.
Generally, the union must have the support of the majority of the group involved to be certified by the Commission as exclusive representative of the group. Once certification is granted, negotiations can begin. The union, on behalf of the employees of the bargaining unit, can require the employer to negotiate in good faith to conclude a collective agreement, which is a document stating the terms and conditions of work as well as the rights and duties of the employer. In the private sector, Mr. Speaker, if it is impossible to come to an agreement after following all these steps and after a certain period determined by law, the employees can exert pressure by initiating a strike and the employer can do the same with a lockout. As soon as the collective agreement is signed, it is binding on each party; there can no longer be a strike during the term of the agreement, and any dispute as to the interpretation and application of the agreement must be settled by submitting the matter to an independent third party, known, as we are all aware, as the arbitrator for grievances.
Bill C-45 follows the restrictive model of the public sector, Mr. Speaker. Strikes are forbidden, disputes in bargaining are settled by arbitration; negotiable issues are restricted; any partisan political activity is forbidden for employee organizations or unions; and in addition, of the great number of people working on Parliament Hill, many are excluded from the collective bargaining system by being designated.
The Bill as a whole applies to people employed by or engaged in work in or for the Senate, the House of Commons, the Library of Parliament, Members of Parliament, and members of the research staff of parliamentary groups, but a number of these people are excluded from the application of Part I whose purpose "is to provide to certain persons employed in parliamentary service, collective bargaining and other rights in respect of their employment". A number of additional restrictions are contained in the preliminary clauses, such as the provision that nothing in Part I shall be construed so as to affect the right or authority of an employer to determine the organization of the employer and to assign duties and classify positions of employment. All this is stated in Bill C-45, but as I said earlier, I shall try, and I hope that the Committee will do the same, to make classification standards negotiable. Persons excluded from Part I are those on the staff of Cabinet Ministers, Senators and Members (employees of the Whip, the Leader of the Opposition or any person in an official position and all those who work for a Member of Parliament). Researchers for parliamentary groups, and persons in temporary employment with a parliamentary committee are also excluded, because they do not come under the definition of "employee", as given in the Bill. Persons appointed by the Governor in Council, part-time, that is working one-third of the normal work period, and casual, working less than six months, and also people in a managerial or confidential position.
After having provided for exceptions, there remains a core of people employed by the House, the Senate and the Library who can enter into collective bargaining. Those persons may be members of an employee organization and participate in the latter's lawful activities. Those activities are protected against any intervention or discrimination by the employer, but they may not take place on the employer's premises during working hours.
Mr. Speaker, the administration of the labour relations system as provided for in Part 1 is the responsibility of the Public Service Labour Relations Board, the tribunal established to administer and adjudicate any matter subject to collective bargaining within the Federal Public Service-that is the body I mentioned earlier-which was established in 1967. The Board has the power to decide over the certification of labour groups, the extent of bargaining units, the hearing of complaints-it establishes rules of procedure both for the adjudication and the settlement of grievances. health, employment and security at work. Previously, as we know, none of those sections of the legislation applied to the House of Commons, to the Senate and still less to the Library.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have looked forward to having some legislation before this House of Commons for many years to provide rights for workers on the Hill.
Members of Parliament have been embarrassed because of incidents that have occurred in these buildings over the years. I have only to refer to the unexpected announcements made by former Speaker Francis when he talked about incidents on the Hill as a result of not having labour protection for people here. This litany of horror stories no other institution would accept, and if they had there would have been prosecutions for unfair labour practices, sexual harassment and so on.

November 1, 1985
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
We have had a rotten borough as far as the rights of workers are concerned. We have one of the last bastions in Canada that has no worker protection.
This legislation moves us a bit along the road to what happens in most workplaces. What annoys me the most, Mr. Speaker, is that we are not setting forward model legislation for our own employees. We are not saying that this is what should be the case in Canada. Parliament Hill, of all places, should be looking after the interests of workers in a fair and equitable manner, but that is not the case in this legislation.
In introducing the legislation, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) admitted that he was taking some parts from the Public Staff Relations Act but not going quite as far as that present Act allows. He was not going to the Canada Labour Code except for Parts III and IV. He is taking a few pieces from each of those major pieces of legislation and putting them together so we can have something for the people on the Hill.
If you look at the abuses mentioned by former Speaker Francis and if you look at what has happened to people working on the Hill, working for us, for the people of Canada, I would say that there is a strong case to be made for a good piece of legislation instead of that which we have before us today. Even now, we are not moving forward on this legislation because of willingness of Members of the House and we are not doing it because we think it is the right thing to do.
Unfortunately, the Government is bringing forward this legislation only because there are cases in front of the Canada Labour Relations Board and our courts which are forcing us to move.
Without any legislative protection whatever, over 1,000 people working on the Hill have joined the Public Service Alliance of Canada. They have done so because of what has happened here. Appointments have been made on the basis of patronage. They have seen nepotism and people getting promoted for granting various favours to their employers. People have seen that happen and they know it is happening. They know also that transfers take place without consultation and reductions in the number of workers take place without any input employees. They know they can be fired or transferred without any grievance procedure. Because of that, they have gone to the Canadian Labour Relations Board and said: "We believe we are Canadian citizens and that we should come under the Canada Labour Code".
The Canada Labour Relations Board listened to the complaints and made a decision that because the House of Commons, the Parliament of Canada, was a federal institution, people on the Hill should have the protection of the Labour Code, and it was in the process of granting a number of groups on the Hill the right to join a union under the protection of the Canada Labour Code. Parliament sat-and may I say it sat on its ass-for years.

Sat on its seat, Mr. Speaker. We are known for sitting, and how we sit is also very well known. We have people in the restaurants and cafeterias, people working as messengers and in the distribution service, people working in the broadcast service, committee reporting service, maintenance, the Library of Parliament, the Senate maintenance and messenger service, the French and English indexes, the staff of Members of Parliament, mainly the New Democratic Party staff, the printing staff, the nurses, the constables and security and the committee clerks all asking to be certified under the Canada Labour Relations Code.
The Government's reaction, and I admit it was supported by all three Parties a year and a half ago, was to bring forward a piece of legislation. We do not believe that the legislation is strong enough. We do not believe the legislation is providing the protection necessary for workers. This legislation is quite weak. This legislation has six major weaknesses.
First, the classification of position in the assignment of duties cannot be dealt with in negotiations. Second, staffing, job appointments, appraisals, promotions, demotions, transfers and lay-offs cannot be dealt with under this legislation. Third, grievance procedures are limited. Grievances cannot go to third party arbitration except in certain circumstances. Fourth, union grievances are not allowed in many areas. Fifth, Members of Parliament staff are excluded from the right of collective bargaining. Sixth, the right to strike is prohibited.
At the present time, certification procedures will require that the thousand or more people who have signed union cards will have to start again from scrath. The people who have had the nerve in this House over the last three years who are working for us with no protection and who have signed union cards in order to take cases forward to the courts about the House of Commons are now having to start all over again. That is plainly unjust. If the Canada Labour Relations Board is right, they have the right to go forward right now with the union cards they have presently. The Government by this piece of legislation will be taking away what they have fought to obtain over the last three years.
I have given notice to the Government House Leader that when we go forward in committee, I would like some indication from him as to whether or not he will act on this very unjust matter. Despite many things which I have said about him in the past, I believe he may act quite favourably in response to this reasonable recommendation. Certainly it would undo an injustice in the legislation.

There are many things I could say and will say about the legislation before my time is up. However, one of the most ironic things about it is that a worker in a support role for the Privy Council, in other words for the Prime Minister's Office, would have more rights under legislation than one working for the Parliament of Canada. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that legally people working in the Privy Council Office have the right to strike? Do you know that they are covered by all aspects of the Public Service Staff Relations Act? Do you recognize that in many parts of Canada we have given people who work for the Government of Canada, for the Supreme Court, for the Governor General and for various Crown corporations, rights which we are denying our own people under this legislation? That is a very serious problem.
Why are we doing it? Are we saying that the Privy Council Office is not an essential service? Some may say that after the last month or two, it might be a good idea if it closed down for a while. Certain Tory back-benchers would probably be quite grateful if it closed down for a while. We are saying that that is not an essential service, but people here are providing essential services. I am not sure whether the messenger service is essential in the way this legislation means it. Certainly it is an essential service to us. However, if they wanted to go out on strike to protect their rights, and if it were the only way in which they could solve a problem, I think we should allow that. If that is the only way in which they can resolve the difference with us, I believe they should have that right.
Before talking about the people covered by the legislation, I should like to spend a few minutes talking about those who will not be covered. Earlier I mentioned that among the groups which applied for certification under the Canada Labour Code were the people who worked for the NDP caucus, the members of our staff on the Hill. The working relationship which we have had with the New Democratic Party caucus staff over the years indicates how things could work for Members. This legislation runs the danger of even taking away the rights which our employees have, the employees of Members of Parliament, at the present time. Right now they have an application before the Canada Labour Relations Board to allow them to have full certification as opposed to the voluntary certification which they have with us. This will be taken away by this legislation.
We have had a collective agreement with our staff since 1977. This agreement has been renegotiated three times. It sets out working conditions for the employees hired by caucus and by individual caucus members. It provides for the resolution of staffing problems through a grievance procedure. It includes the appeal of difficult problems through third party arbitration. I have sat on those appeals, and 1 know they can work. Our collective agreement also provides for agreed procedures for staffing of vacant positions, for technological change, respect for overtime, standards for vacations, education and travel. Our employees understand that they can meet with our caucus and talk about their rights. We think that is something with which we have survived quite well, not without some
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
difficulties, since 1977. There have been over eight years of success through negotiating.
Why is it being said that that cannot happen any more? Why is the Government saying that Liberal and Conservative staff members cannot join a union? The legislation says that they cannot. The Government is taking away an existing right, and I do not think that is fair. I am not sure how the staff of Members of Parliament of the Conservative and Liberal Parties feel about that. It is a problem for us because we have recognized the rights of our employees. We want to ensure that this legislation recognizes their rights as well.
Speaking about the rights of Members of Parliament and explaining why there needs to be some protection, I should like to take a look at what happens in Ministers' offices and in the Privy Council Office, compared with what happens to us as Members of Parliament. At this time we are being asked to do more as Members of Parliament. The Auditor General is saying that we have to do a much better job of keeping Ministers on track in terms of Government spending. Also, reform of Parliament is taking place, indicating that we should be doing more on committees and doing a much more careful job not only of amending legislation but perhaps of introducing our own legislation through the committee system. At the same time the budgets of Members of Parliament are not being increased. 1 see other members of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services in the Chamber this afternoon. We have been fighting for over a year to obtain an increase in the budget for the staff of Members of Parliament. We have had no success. However, at the same time, the Prime Minister's Office has been increased by a third in terms of numbers of people and its budget has gone up by over 50 per cent. Members of Cabinet have increased their staff allocation tremendously, again by over 50 per cent, and have increased the number of people working for them, yet the same has not been done for Members of Parliament. One of the reasons for this happening is that our staff do not have any negotiating power with the administration of the House of Commons. They do not have the right to say: "Look at what is happening, look at the expectations you are putting on us, look at the expectations you are putting on Members of Parliament, look at the new role which is being set out for Members of Parliament. Yet you are not giving us any more money for it". I think that is also a problem.
We also suffer with regard to how Members' staff is treated in comparison with Ministers' staff in the long run. At the present time there is a system in place, whereby people working in Ministers' offices, after a number of years, are able to be integrated into the Public Service, that they will be given preferential hiring for various posistions within the Public Service of Canada.
That is a form of favouritism which can be justified. It is a recognition that someone who has worked in a Minister's office for a number of years has a certain skill, ability and knowledge, and obviously has spent a fair amount of time working for the people of Canada. However, we do not do the same thing when it comes to people who have worked for

November 1, 1985
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
Members of Parliament. For example, someone who has worked in the office of the NDP immigration critic could have spent five years working on immigration problems, and I suspect that one could have spent five years in the last ten months working on those problems. However, if that person wanted to apply for a job in the Department of Employment and Immigration, he or she would not receive any recognition whatsoever. That is an injustice, and it is an injustice that our own employees do not have any particular rights under present legislation and that what they do have will be taken away by the Government.
I do not want to be the only Member who has a chance to speak on the legislation this afternoon, but I have a few other points to make. It is important to realize that we are not setting forth on a new path. What we are doing here is accepting that we are being forced to move along that path. I think that is regrettable. However, what I would like to hear-and I am sure the Minister responsible will tell us about it in committee-is when that will happen. What will happen if there are successful negotiations between the Public Service Alliance of Canada and Treasury Board? If we move away from some of the restrictive provisions of the Public Service Staff Relations Act and guarantee the workers of the Government of Canada some of the protections that are there under the Canada Labour Code, if that happened-and it is certainly something that I fought for for many years-then I want to make sure that this House provides the same protection for the people who work here. I would like to be guaranteed by the Minister responsible for this legislation that the Government will move at the same time for the people who work on the Hill as it moves for the other people who work for the Government of Canada right across this land. In other words, what I am saying is that if there is legislation moving people who are presently under the Public Service Staff Relations Act under the new provisions of the Canada Labour Code, or changing the Public Service Staff Relations Act to include some of the same guarantees as are in the Canada Labour Code, at the same time this Act should be amended so that our people on the Hill will receive those same types of guarantees. I think that is the crux of the matter.
One of the reasons that there has been a fight against this legislation, even before it came before us, is that there is a recognition that, for the people who work on the Hill especially, the Public Service Staff Relations Act is not adequate legislation that will really protect their rights. Under the Public Service Staff Relations Act there are many things that
cannot be negotiated which are the very crux of the problems that people who work on the Hill face. They want to be able to discuss, at a negotiation table, classification of jobs and assignment of duties. They want to able to talk about staffing decisions. They want to be able to grieve staffing decisions to an outside body. That is not possible under this legislation. Some of that is possible under the Public Service Staff Relations Act and some of it is not, but what we are setting up here is that we are accepting the Public Service Staff Relations Act and then we are watering it down.
I want from the Minister, in committee-and I have explained it to him already so it is not a surprise-some guarantee that we are going to move away from this system. I think we have to expect that the Government has a good chance of passing this legislation sometime in the future. The last time I counted Government Members outnumbered us slightly in this House of Commons, 27 to one, so they have a chance-not a good chance but they have a chance-of passing this legislation. But I want guarantees from the Government that when improvements take place for the Public Service of Canada, they should also take place for the people on the Hill, and that it is not just another watered down version of improvements but a real improvement, so that we are protecting the people who work for us and work for the people of Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the adoption of Bill C-45 will prove to be a significant milestone in Canadian parliamentary history.
For the first time ever, Mr. Speaker, the relations between Members, senators, senior parliamentary officials and their staff will be subject to a whole series of rights, obligations and restraints. In addition, a new element-the union movement- will play a leading and legitimate role in these relations.
Whatever the outcome may be, chances are indeed that parliamentary activities will never be the same, and we rejoice for Canadians because extending the rights of our own employees can only enhance this institution.

I would like to reassure the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) that in committee or perhaps even sooner, as the House Leader of the Government said in his speech, we will be considering matters which are concern to him, such as the efforts which have been made up to date by employees to get themselves organized and so on. We will do our utmost so that their good efforts are not wasted. At the same time, we want to protect the rights of all employees, those who up until now have not been interested in the word that was being done to organize them in the existing unions, as well as those who had already accepted that situation.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to make working conditions of parliamentary employees similar to those of their counterparts in the Public Service. It will also give collective
November 1, 1985

bargaining rights to parliamentary employees. For the first time therefore they will enjoy certain rights and some protection.
The Bill is divided in three parts and goes a long way towards improving the labour relations climate on Parliament hill. Part I is similar to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. It designates the Public Service Staff Relations Board as administrator of the act and defines the collective bargaining process, whereas Part II applies Canada Labour Code Part III to parliamentary employees. That part therefore will determine terms and conditions of jobs, including annual leave and working hours. The last part stipulates that Part IV of the Canada Labour Code applies to Parliament employees and determines occupational safety and health standards.
The purpose of Bill C-45 is therefore to create a structure for collective bargaining between the House and its employees. If and when adopted, it will grant Parliament employees the collective bargaining rights normally prescribed in this kind of legislation, including the right to join a union without any fear of reprisals from their employer. Moreover, it will provide all employees with the wide range of rights and guarantees listed in Parts III and IV of the Canada Labour Code, including the right to refuse to do hazardous work, and minimal guarantees concerning vacation leave, maternity leave, working hours, etc. The legislation will provide workers on Parliament Hill with a wide range of rights and regulations, giving them a protection to which they had no access until now. Moreover, Bill C-45 will provide them with more rights than those contemplated in the draft bill which our Committee on Management and Members' Service had supported in 1984.
In two areas, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-45 incorporates through reference Parts III and IV of the Canada Labour Code, extending to Parliament employees the rights granted to all employees under Federal jurisdiction. If we consider, for instance, some of the rules which forbid discrimination for workers under federal jurisdiction, for instance in Crown Corporations, as well as the new Canadian Government contract compliance policy, we can see that making Parts III and IV of the Canadian Labour Code apply to Parliamentary Hill employees, we are certainly giving them more rights than they had before.
The other aspect of Bill C-45 which goes further than the recommendation of the Committee on Management and Members' Services concerns the fact that Parliamentary Hill employees will be covered by the provisions of Parts III and IV of the Code, even though the staff of Members of Parliament, Senators, research services and caucuses will not be covered by the other parts of this Bill. However, they will be subject to Parts III and IV, which means that they will have extended rights and a better protection than the Committee on Manage-
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act ment and Members' Services had recommended in 1984. It is therefore better than what the Committee had recommended.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, some might say, like the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) did earlier, that the Bill does not go far enough. But still upon looking at the history of the protection of the rights of Parliamentary employees, we must realize that indeed this legislation is bringing something very important into the life of those employees, and it will have a rather massive impact on working conditions and environment in Members' offices.
The impact on Members and Senators of the implementation of Parts III and IV of the Code to their staff will be extensive. For instance, if a Member wishes his or her employees to work after the so-called standard hours provided for in Part III of the Code, meaning an average eight hours a day or 48 hours in any week, he or she will need permission from the Minister of Labour. Further, a Member's employee with more than one year of service who is being fired may ask the Minister of Labour to have his dismissal reviewed by a third party. In my view, that is quite a protection. Many of my constituents are civil servants, in the neighbourhood of 17,000, and I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that many representations have been made to me concerning employees that were fired somewhat high-handedly. So this is a protection employees were impatiently waiting for.
Besides, where a Member's employee ... where the dispute cannot be settled through informal mediation, the Minister may submit the matter to a referee who has much more extensive powers, including that of ordering the reinstatement of the employee involved, and this order can even be supported by a Federal Court judgment.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this is something very significant, and very deserving to be noted. It is true that job classification, staffing, and all that, are not covered by this legislation. But when you consider the somewhat unusual relationships that exist between MPs and their staffs and the emergency work that can come up, the very rapidly changing situations, and also sometimes the very special projects that must be dealt with, if Members of Parliament were to be deprived of their freedom to manage their own offices, to allocate tasks to persons who are capable and qualified to deal with them, or, in cases of absence, to be able to transfer people between jobs in order to fill any gap created by reason of illness or whatever, they would be unable to fulfill their duty and would not at that point provide their constituents with the quality of services they promised to deliver when elected, with the commitment to adequately represent their constituents.
Therefore, as Lloyd Francis aptly said, labour relations between Members of Parliament and parliamentary staff must retain some sort of specificity, a character that do not apply, for instance, to other occupations under Federal jurisdiction that are related to transportation, maintenance, or whatever.

November 1, 1985
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
There is something very special about parliamentary work and we must preserve that specific character.
We also recall that conditions altogether different existed between 1908, when the Public Service was established, and 1961, when the permanent staff of the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library of Parliament came under the Public Service Employment Act as far as appointments, classification, salaries and promotions were concerned. However, Parliament kept its control over the duration of employment, the provisions regulating annual leave, standards for work performed outside, etc.
Mr. Speaker, in other words, the employee in those days was not protected as he will be under Bill C-45. Now why should the employees of the Members of Parliament be excluded? In Part I, it is stated that they are excluded from collective bargaining; on the other hand, in Parts II and III of the Bill they are included as I said previously, as parliamentary employees to whom Parts III and IV of the Canadian Labour Code apply.
Therefore, the employees of Members of Parliament will be far better off because they will benefit from improved labour conditions as provided to all employees while enjoying that very special relationship with their bosses which is necessary in parliamentary work.
Mr. Speaker, in addition, the President of the Treasury Board is now undertaking negotiations with unions to amend the Public Service Staff Relations Act. The Government hopes that the amendments to that legislation will also be included in Bill C-45.
The purpose of the Bill before the House today is to bring the working conditions of parliamentary employees up to a level comparable with that of their counterparts in the Public Service. This is another example of the Government's commitment to parliamentary reform, and the emphasis is on fairness in relations between the Government and its employees.
Unfortunately, Bill C-45 does not enshrine all the principles of personnel administration, such as merit, and does not deal with staffing, promotions, transfers, competition, and so forth. Many of my constituents come to my office to complain that they have been treated unfairly in a competition or did not get the promotion they deserved. Their files often contain numerous recommendations attesting that their work is superior and even excellent. However, when it is time for them to move on in their career, their advancement or promotion is stalled as a result of habits that have developed in the last twenty years. Mr. Speaker, if there is anything that demoralizes our public servants, it is that. Corrective action must be taken.
It is clear, therefore, that the principles governing these matters should be dealt with at another level, as recommended by the Auditor General in his 1983 report. We must give careful and speedy consideration, as was said several times in the House, on both sides of the House in fact, to the merit
principle in the Public Service. It is to be hoped that negotiations between the President of Treasury Board and the unions will result in something positive that will truly improve the working conditions of our public servants. And it is also to be hoped that we will be able to reach an amical agreement with the unions so that parliamentary employees, as a result of Bill C-45, will get better working conditions, will feel that their work counts, and that as a result, productivity, which may be slack sometimes in certain areas, will improve. Because you know, Mr. Speaker, that the days when we had an inexhaustible pool of resources that could be used in emergencies when it was necessary to set up special teams to cope with a given situation, those days will soon be over if they are not already.
Mr. Speaker, cutbacks in the Public Service for budgetary reasons must not be made in a cavalier fashion and without consideration for the individual. We must ensure that the staff we have on Parliament Hill is working under conditions that will promote better productivity, high moral and quality service to the public, through its Members.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your attention and, in concluding my remarks, I want to reassure my Opposition colleagues by saying that this Bill is considered as a major piece of legislation by the Government and the Member for Gatineau, indeed by every Member whose riding is home to a great many public and Parliament Hill employees, not simply because those people are electors who will vote in the next elections, but because we know very well that our work as Members is not quite up to par if our employees are demoralized or lack the necessary facilities or assistance, or the favourable environment and surroundings to give the best of themselves.
I therefore hope the Bill will be quickly referred to the legislative committee for closer scrutiny and improvements, as the Government House Leader has already suggested, and that it will be adopted without delay so that our employees may benefit from it and that all of us may be better parliamentary representatives of our electors.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer my colleague. As I said in my remarks, the specific nature of the work done by parliamentary assistants prevents us from considering them as we do all other employees on Parliament Hill. As former House Speaker Francis said when he was faced with the same decision, he had considered, and I will say this in English-

However, Speaker Francis considered the application of the Code to House employees as inappropriate and potentially disastrous for several reasons. For example, the Canada Labour Code does not provide for the continuation of essential services in the event of a strike nor does it in other ways recognize the unique functions and responsibilities of parliamentary institutions. Accordingly, the Speaker responded by seeking from the Federal Court (Trial Division) an order prohibiting the Canada Labour Relations Board from continuing to take jurisdiction.
He said:
"It is evident that Parliament, as an employer, is not like any trucking, rail, shipping, bank, or radio and television company that comes under the Canada Labour Code. The uniqueness of Parliament suggests the need to define a suitable legal framework for granting its employees the right to bargain collectively."

Therefore, that is not quite the case put forward by my hon. friend, but it shows the sort of context in which Parliament employees' rights, privileges and protections were discussed. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that if my hon. friend thought about it seriously, he would realize that there is a big difference between the job of a Paliamentary assistant who must deal sometimes with urgent situation and show initiative, and that of an employee who must perform day in day out the same routine tasks which are assigned to him or her. He is perfectly aware that our employees on Parliament Hill are faced with constantly changing situations. There are really no standard formulas or patterns to define the jobs of our Parliamentary assistants.
He has to reinvent his routine each day because new situations are always coming up. Some constituents might need a certain thing, and he has to reorganize his priorities as well as those of his boss. Because of this, if he were constrained in an
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act administrative straightjacket which did not provide the flexibility he needs to do his job, he could not serve his Member of Parliament as well as he should, and I believe that this would make the employees themselves quite unhappy.
1 discussed this with employees before speaking about this Bill in the House, and they told me that, as long as their working conditions are protected, as long as their work is safe, free of any danger for their health, and so on, as long as there are rules to determine their hours of work, the length of their working day, their holidays, and so on, they are very happy to have different labour relations and conditions than those applying to the maintenance, library or services employees, who wait for people to ask them questions or to request something from them, while our own employees must very often be creative in order to help us, and they would not have the freedom of action necessary if the framework of their job was too restrictive. This is why there are differences between our own employees and other workers on the Hill.

Mr. Speaker, on October 25, 1966, I walked into this building for the first time in my life. On that day I walked up to the sixth floor of this building and asked the maitre d' of the Parliamentary Restaurant for a job. He said: "Yes, we have openings. We have them frequently", and the next day, October 26, I started here as a busboy. That was the first job I had in my life.
1 worked in this building from 1966 until I left to become a Member of the Ontario Legislature in 1981. Of course, for that period of time I had two jobs. I was an employee of this House as well as being in a municipal office in the Township of Cumberland prior to my election in 1981.
The job I did in the beginning as a busboy was not as glamorous or as highly paid as other jobs. The job of busboy at that time paid $2,368 per year. I still have the stub of my first pay cheque and last night when I was reviewing my notes to speak today 1 examined it very closely. Needless to say, with that kind of salary it was difficult to keep busboys and other employees here for any more than a few weeks. There was a very high rate of turnover among the employees of the restaurant and certain other departments.
When I came back here in the fall of 1984, I noticed that there had been considerable change in the three and a half years I had been absent from Parliament Hill. Notwithstanding the fact that the salaries were not all that great when I was an employee here, there was, nevertheless, a good feeling among staff members on the Hill, whether they were blue-collar or white-collar workers. The staff, regardless of where they worked, felt good about working here because this was and, of course, still is, a very special and unique place to work. It was a privilege to be able to work here, at least that was the feeling felt by the employees when they worked here. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be able to say a few words about this Bill because I was a plant worker and a union member for eighteen years. In fact, 1 was secretary of my union for two years and this subject has a special interest for me.

The arguments we have heard against allowing full union rights to the majority of employees of Parliament are very old arguments that have been disproved time and time again. A hundred and fifty to 200 years ago we heard the same sort of argument essentially from the industrial employers of Great Britain.
The same people who argued that they would go broke if 10 year old children were not allowed to work in the mines also argued they would go broke if their employees were allowed to have unions. It is less than two centuries since membership in any union in any industry was a crime. There was the famous case of the Tolpuddle Martyrs, agricultural workers. People in every country have to eat. I guess the argument was that those six or seven agricultural workers who committed the crime according to the statutes of the day of paying a shilling or two apiece membership dues in a union were threatening to starve all the people of England. In fact, the people of England decided that that was not so. Eventually the Government had to allow them to come home again, except one of them decided he had had enough of England and he came and settled in London, Ontario. In fact, at every stage, workers have been told: "We can't let you form a union because it would be disastrous to our industry", or in this case, disastrous to the Government of the country.
The attitude, of course, is that workers are a foolish, wicked, irresponsible lot who cannot be trusted to do an honest job. If they got a little power through being able to join together, the same power that the owners of capital exercise all the time, to counterbalance that power, then it would bring the country to ruin.
By the end of the last century, most workers in Britain were organized into unions and Britain reached the peak of its well-being in many respects according to most historians at that time. The workers of most of the western countries who have organized unions, often at the cost of martyrdom, death, imprisonment, harassment, are in countries now considered to be leading in prosperity and leading in good order. It is not only a matter of whether union members are satisfied enough

November 1, 1985
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
to work, it is also a matter of whether a person has the recognized dignity to speak in terms of moral equality with his or her employer.
In my 18 years as a factory labourer it was very important, not just to me, but to all others in the factory that a worker knew that his or her right to speak as an independent human being was protected by the union which was founded on law, the laws of Ontario. It did not mean that a worker did not have to work. The union could not protect a worker who was slacking. It did not mean that a union member could violate the ordinary relationship, insult the foreman or something like that. It did mean that the foreman could not insult the worker. It did mean that the foreman could not drive the worker mercilessly. It did mean that there were rules applicable to both sides, that both sides had to observe.
The rules were broken on both sides from time to time. From time to time management and supervisors did what was wrong. From time to time union members did what was wrong. There was a system for adjudicating those. There were disciplinary procedures jointly recognized. There were grievance procedures jointly recognized. We had recourse to arbitration. We did not do it very often but once in a year or two the union might take a case to arbitration. We might win it or we might lose it. It was healthy because it kept the company on its toes and it kept the union on its toes.
We had to be serious about our grievances to make sure that we had what we thought was a reasonable case. The company had to be serious about its answers because it knew if it simply ignored an honest case, the company could get smacked down in arbitration. There are millions of workers in Canada who enjoy that kind of protection today. It is one of the things that makes Canada a healthy, prosperous and peaceful country.
Forty years ago that was not the case. Forty years ago during the latter part of the Depression when the unions were organizing, there was the potential for utter chaos. We had the then Premier of Ontario bringing mounted troups in to smash up the union organizing in the City of Oshawa of General Motors and so on. He got tossed out in the next election of course. He was wrong, and the voters said he was wrong.
What was established then in North America generally as the pattern of labour law was the concept of the contract. It is not necessarily the same in Britain or in Europe but in the United States and Canada for forty years, on the pattern of the Wagner Act, we have had a deal. The deal is for the life of a contract, let us say for a year, the company agrees that it will pay certain wages, maintain certain conditions and will not change them except by mutual agreement with the union. In return, the union agrees that it will not strike. It will not indirectly strike through an organized slow-down or disruption. For one year, or it can be for longer, there is labour peace. That was the basic pattern worked out. It has worked very, very well. Far more than 90 per cent of union negotiations are carried on within that general concept to a conclusion without a strike, certainly without the bitterness of violence on the picket line-carried out to a conclusion that is never perfect but is normally found to be workable. I mean, at the end of
contract negotiations between the executive of my local in which I sat and the management, the general feeling was: Well, it was not all we wanted, but we can live with it, and we did. It saved a great deal of heartache, and it meant that employees and managers or supervisors could talk to each other with mutual respect. I did not have to be afraid that the manager or the supervisor could trample on my rights. I did not have to be so defensive, and he knew that I could go so far within my rights as a human being but no farther, that we would not try to wreck the place economically. We recognized that we wanted jobs there next year too. There was an atmosphere of peace and stability created by the assistance of the union and the contract arrived at. That method of arriving at it included not only recourse to arbitration; it included even the right to strike. There were times when we took a strike vote. While I was there, we never in fact did go on strike, but we had that possibility and we could contemplate whether or not we thought it was in our interests to do it. In fact, when we took strike votes, and the strike vote gave the executive a mandate, we never chose to go out on strike and the company never chose to exercise its corresponding right of lock-out. The system works, not perfectly, but far better than anything that went before it.
The trouble with this Parliament is that it is living in the beginning of the 19th century in which it is afraid of its own employees. This Parliament, collectively speaking, fears truck drivers, bus drivers, waitresses, cleaners, security men, constables and clerks. It fears those people. It says that if they are allowed to have the same freedom as is enjoyed by law by all other workers in Canada or practically-let us say more than 90 per cent of other workers in Canada-if we allow our employees to have the human rights that the huge majority of Canadians enjoy, well, we could not do our job as a Parliament; we could not run the country, supposing that it is Parliament that runs this country. There is some ground for questioning that when we see how impossible t is for us to get information about how the country is being run. That is another problem. Supposing this Parliament does run this country, what we are being told on the opposite side is that that would be impossible, if we allowed truck drivers and bus drivers and people like that on the Hill the right to strike. It is a ridiculous proposition which goes against all the experience in Canada, the United States, Britain and most western countries.
Because public opinion and the courts and boards like labour relations boards are crowding us, the Government has decided it has to do something. It is doing it as slowly as possible. It has sabotaged the original organizing effort by our employees by introducing a Bill to block it and to give decidedly less rights than our employees were entitled to under the Canada Labour Code. It has sabotaged any possibility of the employees of this Parliament doing what the employees of the Ontario Legislature are able to do, and some of them are doing, namely, create a union as free people. It has ruled that that is impossible.
November 1, 1985

Considering the poor wages, the unjust working conditions, the patronage and so on, which has been much better explained by my colleague from Churchill and by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), whom I respect highly for his authority in his knowledge as a worker on this subject, in spite of the known, rotten conditions and rotten relationships at work, we still refuse to allow-that is, this Government and, therefore, the Parliament it controls- our employees to have the rights that practically all other Canadians enjoy. I agree with the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell that we do not necessary have to say that it is all or nothing. Every management jurisdiction that uses the labour relations system established throughout North America has the right to claim certain exclusions. There are certain employees or certain positions within which the employees may not come within the jurisdiction of the union.
The president of a company has to have a secretary who can type a letter from him to the union if the union is on strike- that is the ultimate example-since the president of the company, of course, would not demean himself by typing his own letter, if he could. That is not a problem. If the issue here were which of the positions should be excluded, a minority of management-type positions being excluded, we could discuss that and, I believe, arrive at a reasonable agreement. There would be some borderline cases, and we might go this way this year and that way next year on some of them, according to experience. That principle is well established, and everybody here who has worked anywhere else knows that that principle is well established. The principle of job classification is well established. It is not a disruption of management's rights.
The company I worked for, Continental Can, which insisted on bringing in a much more sophisticated job classification system and job evaluation system. It wanted it. The union resisted it for a while, and then we finally accepted a system in a modified form. The company felt it was better off. Instead or arguing with each individual about whether he should get a nickel more or a dime more in his job, the company wanted it done by a recognized set of criteria.
I want to say a little bit now about our experience in the NDP caucus. As a trade unionist, I and some others have found it embarrassing to say that sometimes we have engaged in an activity, perhaps thoughtlessly, which we would not tolerate and did not tolerate when we were on the other side of the table in our bargaining as union members or representatives. We got brought up short by our union, the Parliamentary Association of Support Staff. It was embarrassing, but in fact the relationships have been improved since then and there was an equality established, a moral equality. I am still the employer in my office, but I am not an absolute monarch, and I do not want to be. I could not handle it. I believe the same would apply to all other Members of this Parliament. Having a union to represent the employees, even though each Member is the employer under the present rules, is not uncommon. That happens in the fur industry, in the boot and shoe industry, in many industries and small factories-one union and one employer's association, and that is the model we are using in
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act our caucus. We might find better models, but it would in fact not only bring justice to a thousand employees on the Hill, but it would bring a much more stable working relationship to the employers on the Hill and Members of Parliament, and we would then be able to hold up our heads instead of being ashamed of being one of the worst employers in Canada.

I am very proud of the fact that in 1947, almost 40 years ago, the Government of that day in my province, under the respected and lauded person of one Tommy Douglas, granted collective bargaining rights to all the employees of Crown corporations, the Public Service and the legislature employees of the Province of Saskatchewan.

speechtext:

Since 1935, this matter has been raised in Parliament, as I said earlier to my colleague from the Liberal caucus when I was asking a question. In fact there were even some members from the Progressive Party in the 1920s, whom I know my honourable friend from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) will recall, even though he is younger than I am, who raised the same matter back then, but especially since 1935, and the Government of the day gave the darndest variety of reasons and excuses and protests that you could imagine. Quite often, and I have even had this experience in this House since 1968, when the matter was raised my colleagues from the Conservative Party agreed with us and supported us because of those darn, mean, miserable old Liberals sitting on the other side of the Chamber.
