speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, Notices of Ways and Means Motions should be drafted in plain language and that the practice of incorporating complicated draft tax bills into the text of such notices be discontinued.
He said: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext: Explain!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has just requested that I explain. That is precisely what I intend to do over the next 20 minutes.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext: In plain language.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext:
In plain language. 1 know no other, Sir.
What brought about my putting of this motion on the Notice Paper was the receipt on my desk on September 9, not too long ago, of a Notice of Ways and Means Motion dealing with proposed changes to the Income Tax Act. This Notice of Ways and Means Motion reads as follows: "That it is expedient to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to make a related amendment to the Tax Court of Canada Act as follows," and what follows, Sir, is a draft Bill of some 240 pages in length consisting of complext gobbledegook, for want of a more parliamentary word.
The Income Tax Act is the most complex, complicated and technical statute we have on the books. If we wanted to find out what this Notice of Ways and Means Motion was about, we would have to put the draft Bill side by side with an
November 1, 1985

existing compilation of the Income Tax Act and compare the two. It would probably take a week to find out what it was all about. This should not be necessary and I will try to show in my argument that it runs contrary to the spirit of the rules of the House and contrary to the procedure which is very often correctly adopted by the Government to bring down Ways and Means Motions in such a way that people can read them find out what changes are proposed to these very complicated tax statutes.
Although my motion is pretty specific and deals only with the drafting of Ways and Means Motions, it is part of a greater whole, the whole question of simplicity and comprehensibility in legislation. It should be that any person of reasonable intelligence and comprehension of either the English or French languages ought to be able to read a statute and know what the law is and what penalties are imposed for any infraction of that law. One should not have to have experts like accountants or lawyers to interpret a law. Any citizen should be able to read through a statute book and know what the law means.
Just this morning as an exercise I went through the Criminal Code. Statutes that were drafted many years ago were drafted in simple language and made sense. We can understand what they say. I looked at Section 72 of the Criminal Code dealing with duelling. Everything I could want to know about the legality or illegality of duelling and the penalties imposed for it takes eight lines-and some of those lines are only one word long-in my copy of Martin's Criminal Code.
The Section of the Criminal Code dealing with the unlawful movement of monuments and survey boundary lines takes 23 lines. In the Good Book, I think it takes one line and says something like: "Thou shalt not move the monuments of thy forefathers". The Criminal Code can say the same thing in 23 lines and that ain't bad. Turning to recent legislation, the statutes and commentaries that deal with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol take something like 30 pages of Martin's. It ought not to be that way.
The people who are drafting statutes these days do so in the most esoteric manner possible. They aim for such a degree of precision that it does not make sense any more. They try to contemplate in the law every possible conceivable technical eventuality. This leads to all kinds of technical defences in courts of law that need further expounding by the courts themselves. We do not solve any problems by going into great detail in the statute itself. All we do is make it worse and create the need for yet more interpretations by the courts.
There are frequent complaints about the complexities of legal drafting. These complaints usually come from the Opposition. It does not matter which Party is Opposition, these complaints come from the Opposition. When members of the Opposition get to this side of the House, they tend to forget about these complaints, that being human nature, I suppose. However, in certain jurisdictions these complaints have become organized. There is a movement toward plain language legislation. I understand that this movement is quite active in the United States of America and Australia. I understand that
Ways and Means Motions
in certain states of Australia, when a law is brought in there must also be a plain-language explanation of what that law is all about. Where the request for plain language legislation is becoming more organized, the chances of having plain-language legislation are much greater than they appear to be in Canada at this time.
I would hope that soon it will be taught by the law schools to those who would become drafters of laws that the best way of doing something is usually the simplest way of doing it. When people who are taught that way are hired by the Department of Justice, they will then have that in mind when drafting Bills. They will win points for shortening a proposed law rather than lengthening it.
I return to the issue at hand, the question of the drafting of Ways and Means Motions. The rules as they exist in the House of Commons about the Business of Supply and the Business of Ways and Means make very little sense. They would never have been put together the way they are if they were done as a result of rational thought on this subject. They are like Alice in Wonderland or Topsy, they just growed.
I suppose we would have to go back in history to find out what the Business of Supply and the Business of Ways and Means was all about in the past. We can do that by taking as an example a Parliament of some European country several hundred years ago. The monarch would approach Parliament and say: "I have a new venture in mind. It is an expensive venture. Perhaps we will invade the next country and it will require more money than that which normally accrues to the Crown by the existing taxes". The monarch would make his pitch to Parliament and say that he has had the matter looked at by the Lord Chief Justice and has been assured of its legality and that he has had the matter looked at by a Conference of Bishops and has been assured that it is a just and holy cause. Of course, there will be certain spoils of victory to be divided by those who support this venture. The legislature of the day would resolve itself into a committee of supply and debate the requested amount of money. They might increase it or decrease it a bit and perhaps even vote for it. The next stage would be to find out how the money would be forthcoming. They would again resolve themselves into a committee of Ways and Means and debate the best method of raising the money. It might be necessary to put an extra tax on the peasants or an extra tax on imports such as tobacco or ardent spirits. They would decide among themselves the best way of raising these revenues. Out of that committee of Ways and Means would come a resolution suggesting that taxes be increased on tobacco products, or whatever it might be. A Bill would be drafted after that dealing with the wishes of the resolution which would then go through the legislature in the same fashion as any other Bill.
This type of system was incorporated into early Canadian practice. It involved the principles of free debate upon matters relating to the collection of revenue from the citizens of the

November 1, 1985
Ways and Means Motions
country. There is an interesting quotation from Bourinot which states:
The cardinal principle, which underlies all parliamentary rules and constitutional provisions with respect to money grants and public taxes is this-when burthens are to be imposed on the people, every opportunity must be given for free and frequent discussion, so that parliament may not, by sudden and hasty votes, incur any expenses, or be induced to approve of measures, which may entail heavy and lasting burthens upon the country.
In these days of executive constraint we have changed over a period of time. The idea of a free and independent committee of Ways and Means no longer exists. Not long after the establishment of a Canadian Parliament it was held that only a Minister of Finance could, for example, bring in Ways and Means resolutions. Despite this type of encroachment, at least until 1968 when the great changes were made in parliamentary procedure, the concept was always that tax Bills should be based on Ways and Means resolutions. Again, I would like to quote from Bourinot, page 439 of the Fourth Edition:
When the resolutions amending the tariff, or imposing any changes upon the people, have been agreed to, they are embodied in one or more bills which should pass through the same stages as other bills-
If we look to the Standing Orders of the House of Commons, in particular Standing Order 65(11), we will see that it reads:
The adoption of any Ways and Means motion shall be an order to bring in a bill or bills based on the provisions of any such motion.
Thus, the concept is there. There is a resolution which came out of the Ways and Means Committee and the Bill was to be based on that resolution. However, matters have changed, perhaps for the worst in 1968, to which I have previously referred.
I would now like to quote from the recently published House of Commons Precis of Procedure which was put out by the Table Research Branch of the House of Commons. I think this publication will quoted many times in the House, just as we often refer to Bourinot, Erskine May, or any of the established reference works. It is a very useful document which the Table Research Branch has put forward. With respect to the 1968 changes the document reads as follows:
With the changes to the Standing Orders in 1968, Ways and Means motions replaced the traditional resolutions of the Committee of Ways and Means.
Further down on the page, page 95, we will see another change which was snuck in which reads as follows:
Notices of Ways and Means motions are sometimes tabled in the form of draft bills.
That is what I am trying to get at today. I do not think this practice should take place except perhaps when the Bill is extremely simple. We can see the way the executive part of Government has encroached upon the previous powers which were held by Parliament and that there has been a change in concept. Today we wonder what the point is of the Ways and Means motions which are now put before the House. There does not seem to be any real reason for them. In fact, certain jurisdictions do not use that system at all. The tax Bill just comes in straight to the first reading stage and is not dealt with any differently from any other type of legislation. The Northwest Territories from whence I hail uses that system.
There is no such thing as a Ways and Means motion in the legislature of the Northwest Territories.
If we are to have it, then we must ask ourselves what useful function a Ways and Means motion serves. The answer has to be that it puts down in an understandable form, at least to tax practitioners if not the public or Members of Parliament in general, what it is that the Government wishes to accomplish by the Bill which will be brought in later. We can see that when the Government uses that type of procedure things work out pretty well. When the Budget of last May 23 was brought down, regardless of whether or not one agrees with the specific contents of it, the notice of Ways and Means that was tabled on that day was an excellent piece of work. One can read through the document, which is just a few pages, and find out precisely and exactly what it was the Government wished to accomplish with the legislation it would bring in later. Obviously, there was a good deal of thought which went into the drafting of this notice of Ways and Means. In fact, I would like to compliment the people who put it together.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was in the House not too long ago and I would have liked to have been able to bring that matter to his attention. That is the way we ought to go. That is the way which is the historically right way. It is in keeping with the traditions of the House. It is in keeping with the concepts which have developed over the years. It makes sense. It is a useful procedure for Members of Parliament and for those in the tax community, which includes just about everyone in the country. One can tell from the notice of Ways and Means motion of May 23 exactly what will happen whether one likes it or not. However, that is not the case all the time. The Government sometimes tends to be somewhat lazy. I am sure that is the real reason for it. Perhaps those drafting the legislation feel rushed. One can see that when they come in with a notice of^Ways and Means such as they did on September 9, to which I referred in the initial part of my presentation, it is absolute gobbledegook. It is impossible to understand what they are up to and what they are trying to hide. It makes no sense whatsoever.
The purpose of my motion which is before the House today is to encourage the Government to do it the way it did on May 23 when it brought down the Budget. Some attention should be given to these matters, the intent of what must necessarily be very complex tax legislation should be written down in a way which all of us can understand with just a little bit of effort. Were the Government to do that the House of Commons and the country at large would be well served. We would at least know what the intent of the Government is with respect to tax Bills brought before the House.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have listened with interest for the past 20 minutes to my hon. friend from Western Arctic. I have been listening to my hon. friend for many years and I think, honestly, that this is the first time I have agreed with his position. Perhaps this is the beginning of a breakthrough in the House of Commons. I must say I have listened to his comments and found myself in agreement with almost everything he said. I compliment the
November 1, 1985

Hon. Member for bringing forward Motion No. 234. This is a step toward clarification and a step towards democracy. It will institute real democracy in this House of Commons.
I would like to begin by reading from a recent notice of Ways and Means. 1 would like to read it for those Hon. Members, because of their special interests in various aspects of work being done by Members of the House of Commons. Perhaps Hon. Members do not have the opportunity to read carefully through the notices of Ways and Means motions but just as a sample, Mr. Speaker, and I know how interested you are in this topic, I will share with you how we spend our evenings. 1 will quote a short paragraph of explanation as to what the Government plans to do with taxation:
That the rate per litre specified in any enactment founded on paragraph 11 of this motion for the goods listed in subparagraph (d) of that paragraph be adjusted quarterly on the first day of January, April, July and October of each year, commencing on October 1, 1985, so that the rate applicable during the quarter commencing on any such adjustment day is equal to the rounded product of the rate that would have been applicable if no adjustment had been made pursuant to any enactment founded on this paragraph and the ratio, adjusted or altered in such manner as may be prescribed by regulation of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance and rounded, that the Industry Selling Price Index for Diesel Fuel for the twelve month period ending on the last day prior to the immediately preceding quarter bears to the Industry Selling Price Index for Diesel Fuel for the twelve month period ending on March 31, 1985.

speechtext: Would you explain it?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) asks me to explain it. I must admit, Mr. Speaker, I would have a great deal of difficulty doing so. I believe it simply emphasizes the point made by the Hon. Member that if this is a notice of what the Government intends to do, what on earth is the Government intending to do? I must admit that I, and my staff who are extremely knowledgeable in tax matters, have sat down and poured over this paragraph trying to determine what it means, with no success. I know there must be someone in the rabbit-warrens of the tax Department who understands this, but 1 have yet to find out who that person is.
In a democracy, the assumption is that the electorate will be well informed, and, therefore, make a wise and intelligent decision. That same attitude is transferred to the House of Commons after elections take place so that those people who represent the people of Canada, the duly-elected individuals, can make decisions in the House of Commons based on a thorough understanding of all of the facts and information available. When a Government introduces the Ways and Means motions, it is to alert Members of Parliament and the people of Canada to legislation which will flow out of the Ways and Means motion-it sort of serves notice that this is what it plans to do-and it is not very helpful at all. In fact, what it does is leave the impression that there is almost a
Ways and Means Motions
cover-up being attempted here on the theory that if one uses enough bafflegab and mumbo-jumbo-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext: I am not suggesting that there is some evil intent. But you have to admit, Mr. Speaker, that if the citizenry is to be alerted to tax changes using this kind of language, no one is going to be alerted. If the intentions is honourable and the intent is to inform people of the intentions of the Government, surely, there are not two people in the world who would suggest that this is the way to do it, with the exception of a couple of folks ferreted away down in the catacombs of the Finance Department or the Department of Revenue.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext: It's great for the tax lawyers and accountants.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   WAYS AND MEANS MOTIONS LANGUAGE USED IN DRAFTING
speechtext:
It is a good make-work initiative for tax accountants.
Basically, we have seen some breakthroughs. 1 want to give credit where credit is due. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) did introduce a tax expenditure plan which was an effort, and I believe an honest effort, to identify the major tax expenditures, particularly in the corporate sector, so that Members of Parliament could evaluate each and every one in order to determine if there was any benefit at all accruing to the people of Canada as a result of this tax expenditure. It becomes woefully obvious when we look at many of these phrases that we really have to struggle to make a case that this is actually benefiting Canada as opposed to benefiting a few corporate planners in terms of financial planning. Nevertheless, it is a step in the right direction and I applaud the Minister for that step. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) indicated that there has been on the odd occasion an explanation of the Ways and Means motions which have been proposed so that rather then having to try to get through this gobbledegook, there was some effort to explain what a particular section was trying to say. The explanation used a similar language, unfortunately, but there was still a recognition that there was a problem. 1 think what the motion before us indicates clearly is that we are trying to say to the Government, and to those people who provide us with these motions, that they can be and ought to be written differently and in a fashion so that ordinary Canadians and Members of Parliament who are examining these Ways and Means motions can understand precisely what they are all about.
I would like to conclude my comments today by saying that I believe the intent of this motion is extremely critical. It comes at a very important time. It is both appropriate and timely. It is timely in that we are being asked to debate and to examine so many tax proposals. I suspect that in the weeks and months ahead we will be seeing notice of Ways and Means motions coming before the House on a regular basis as the Government attempts to shift and change the tax system, in a

November 1, 1985
Ways and Means Motions
sense making it more complex at a time when we all would like to see a movement toward a more simplistic tax system.
It is also very appropriate in that there is a sense in the country now that the tax system is unfair, that people do not understand the tax system. I suppose one could say that there is probably not a single Canadian who could honestly say that he or she understand the Tax Act in totality. It is an impossibility. All one could hope for is that the entire Tax Act could be programmed so the computer could access the portions of the Tax Act which would be applicable to an individual or a corporate circumstances. However, at the moment it is so complex there is a feeling it is very biased. Consequently, much of our economy is moving underground because people are avoiding tax. Ordinary Canadians, recognizing that it is an unfair system, and that they are being asked to pay an unfair burden of the tax payments, indulge in many more transactions on an ongoing basis which are unreported. They are almost operating on a barter system or the transaction is completed with cash so there are no records of it. I suspect that most Members of Parliament have encountered people who are in fact continuing this practice as almost a way of life.
What that tells us, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a limit when the system breaks down, that as more and more people take steps, in a sense, to avoid paying tax, those few people who cannot take those steps have to pay more and more and assume an unfair burden in taxes and eventually the system breaks down. I believe we are seeing the beginning of that process now in the country of Italy where so much of the economy is underground and every single citizen is involved in tax finagling, and that is something to behold.
At the time when this mood, this mind-set, is developing in the country, which is extremely destructive in terms of the long-term effective functioning of Parliament, this motion is indeed timely. It is an attempt to make public the Government's intentions so that we can determine in a serious way whether it is appropriate, for example, to increase taxes on, for instance, alcohol. Or is it appropriate to increase the taxes on gasoline? Is it appropriate to lift the sales tax another percentage point? We should explain it in such a way that you can have a sense of national discussion over coffee in the kitchens of Canada so that the word can get back to Members of Parliament for intelligent and informed discussions in the appropriate committees and in the House of Commons. If no one knows what the Government is going to do until the actual Bill arrives in the House, and we are restricted to a half a dozen witnesses before a legislative committee, the purpose then becomes a mockery. It becomes a farcical, nonsensical exercise and it builds on the attitude of the people of Canada that there is something going on here that is not quite right, that there is something inappropriate going on in terms of how the tax system is being developed. I applaud the Hon. Member who introduced Motion 234. As one of the spokespersons on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I say that we will certainly endorse this motion and would like to see an early change in Government policy as a result of it.
Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson)-1 have been told there is no French translation-deals in his motion with matters that are of considerable importance, both to the House of Commons and to the Canadian public in general.
I believe it is a generally accepted fact that our tax laws are not necessarily clearly understood by all Members of this House, and that it would not be an exaggeration to say that the general public in Canada does not directly grasp all the implications of the complex provisions of the Income Tax Act.
Not long ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said quite seriously, when he brought down the last Budget, that one of his most, I would almost say human objectives in the Budget was to make his Budget understandable, and to make all previous Budgets or previous legislation, especially that concerned with income tax, understandable for the general public.
I remember when I was teaching at the University of Montreal, we had an old professor who was giving us a course in didactics before we were to go off and teach our various disciplines. For instance, I was teaching engineering to architects, and it was pretty difficult, and he had explained the difference between complicated and complex.
We were told that something was complex when it was complicated but understandable, while complicated meant something complex that we failed to understand. And I think that reflects the essence of this debate.

I should state right now, of course, that I do not support the direct proposal of this resolution. Although I respect the motives of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), my conclusion after studying this resolution is that his proposal would not have positive results. It would run counter to some of the advances that have been achieved recently in terms of dealing with tax legislation. I am afraid that it would hinder rather than help the goal of legislating better tax laws and it would make things more difficult for taxpayers. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, when our Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs met recently, I had the opportunity for the first time in my life to study thoroughly a proposal to amend a number of regulations, even legislation dealing with extremely complex matters such as financial institutions. Because several of us were new members, expert witnesses and former members in the area had to explain to us the gist of the legislation and procedure.
November 1, 1985

It is clear that it would be impossible to define all the reasons behind a difficult legislation such as the Income Tax Act in one single statement, it is necessary to define them further by associating them with considerations about the lives of the Canadian people which are becoming increasingly more complex in the various regions.

The resolution advocates that plain language should be used in drafting the Ways and Means motions that are introduced and on which the Bill incorporating the precise Income Tax Act amendments is based.
I am sure that no Member of the House would argue against the use of plain language, so long as this language gets the message across clearly and completely. As Members know, when a Budget is presented, the notices of Ways and Means motions that are tabled at the time outlining tax changes in the Budget are in the so-called short form. These notices of motions must include all the essential elements of tax proposals that will be later included in a more detailed Bill, but they are generally in ordinary language rather than the more complex legal language that is used in writing the precise amendments to the Income Tax Act.

I would like to recall what happened in the House this week. It was alleged that some people had taken advantage of every kind of so-called legislative loopholes or dodging mechanisms, and that certain corporations employing crafty lawyers- experts as well, we have to admit-had been able to milk the legislation dry, so to speak, for everything it was worth in their particular sphere of activities.
You can imagine how the legislation could be interpreted if we had to stick to questions of principle only! Everything would then become a contentious issue and the courts would have to rule on every single piece of legislation, never mind the fact that they are overburdened as it is and the source of two-or three-year delays, sometimes even four, five or six years.
I think we would be ill advised to use the kind of language commonly heard on the street-rather vague and replete with generalities-to draft Bills related to highly specialized subjects.

I am not sure whether the language of these notices of motions is plain enough to suit all Members. It could be said that the notice of motion must serve two goals. It has to be clearly understood and it must be adequate in legal terms to serve as the basis for a subsequent Bill. It is not always easy to meet the latter goal while still using simple and clear language. However, that is what the legal drafting people strive for.
I should add, as is generally known, that the supplementary information which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) normally tables with his Budget provides further explanations, in clear language, of the tax changes proposed in the Budget.
Obviously, it is of great importance that tax changes proposed in a Budget be understood clearly, quickly, completely
Ways and Means Motions
and fully. Individuals and businesses need to know where they stand in relation to the new proposals. Often, business decisions, investments and other expenditures hinge on them. The language in both the Ways and Means motions and in the supplementary information must be as clear as possible. Of course, some tax measures are inevitably complex and do not lend themselves easily to simple explanations.
Up to this point in the process, however, there is no disagreement with the principle of the resolution we are debating now. The language must be as clear and plain as possible. What the resolution appears to object to is the further step in the process, which has developed in recent years, of replacing the short form of a Ways and Means motion with a detailed Ways and Means motion. This so-called detailed Ways and Means motion in fact is written in the precise legal terminology that is later used for the Bill itself. Quite obviously, it is not the plain and simple language, as shown in the example given to us by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), which is advocated in the resolution we are debating now. It is written in a manner which attempts to define, very precisely, what is the taxpayer's liability.
Let me remind Hon. Members that the Minister of Finance has said on many occasions that he strongly advocates the simplification of the tax laws as an important goal. That, of course includes simpler language whenever possible, but we should not delude ourselves that achieving this is an easy matter. In our legal tradition an individual's tax liability is determined by the strict letter of the law rather than by the general spirit and broad purpose of the legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to explain to you, and it must be explained to everyone, I think, that the House of Commons here, as I found out, must state basic principles, and we must fight for basic principles, but we must also rely on people from all professions to explain the major purposes of a legislation. Sometimes they are doctors, sometimes they are engineers, but most of the time they are lawyers. But we must not rely on the advice of lawyers only, we also have tax experts who may have an accounting, a business and indeed a legal background. We have engineers involved in some public work Bills that I had an opportunity to examine. In some Bills dealing with health and welfare, we have had descriptions that would look horrible to us, certain medical descriptions written in terms which the average person and even some medical doctors in this House do not understand.
All this is to suggest that our tax system must be comprehensive, it must be specialized in order that it may be used as an unequivocal basis by those who have to enforce it.

The alternative leads to uncertainty and the possibility of arbitrary rulings by tax assessors, so I think we have to accept a certain degree of complexity and rather difficult language in our tax statutes.

November 1, 1985
Ways and Means Motions
The resolution before us apparently complains of the introduction of this precise legal language in the detailed Ways and Means motions which are sometimes placed before the House. There are some very valid and important reasons for doing it in that way. One important factor, which I alluded to earlier, is the importance of enabling taxpayers to know, as early as possible, in a very precise way, what their tax liability would be as the result of a proposed budgetary tax change. Often the taxpayer or his technical adviser can only calculate the tax liability once he has seen the exact language of the proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act. The general language of the short form Ways and Means motion is not always adequate for this purpose. If the taxpayer is not given this certainty, this precision of language, the result can be uncertainty about whether to take certain investment or other economic decisions. When this uncertainty affects many taxpayers, the result can be seen in terms of a slowdown in business, a fall off in investment spending, and other negative effects in the economy. Therefore, it can be important for economic reasons to place detailed Ways and Means motions before Parliament as quickly as possible.
Another reason can be found in the approach that the Government is following of basing policies and actions on the broadest possible consultation with Canadians. This consultation process has been developed in relation with the development of major economic strategies and programs. The National Economic Conference of last spring is an obvious example as is the round of pre-Budget consultations which the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) have again launched. Members will be aware of the two consultation documents presented early yesterday by the Minister which provide a progress report on the Government's strategy for securing economic renewal and a new study of the factors underlying the approach to deficit reduction and control of the national debt. That process of consultation is important, too, in the process of taxing draft legislation. The Minister of Finance has made it clear that he welcomes the advice and counsel of tax experts in the private sector so that our tax amendments are well and soundly written.
A year ago in a speech to the Canadian Tax Foundation the Minister of Finance encouraged tax specialists and practioners to help the Government in simplifying and improving our tax legislation. When it comes to legislating budgetary tax changes, that process of consultation is made much easier by the practice of placing detailed Ways and Means motions before Parliament. This allows private sector tax experts to see the exact language which the Government is contemplating for the subsequent Bill to amend the Income Tax Act. This private sector assistance can be most valuable in achieving sound, practical, well-drafted tax legislation. The tax consultation process would be much more difficult if we did not put the draft legislation forward in this way.
Before concluding this speech, I would like to remind the House of a number of other measures which the Government and the Minister of Finance in particular have taken to improve our tax legislation and the legislative process. I have
referred to the importance placed on the consultation process and also on the goal of tax simplification, one of our ongoing objectives. For example, in his Budget speech last May the Minister of Finance put forward important proposals to restructure the corporate tax system. He invited comments and suggestions from the private sector as part of the ongoing process of public consultation. It is also important to note that the proposals to change the corporate tax system were motivated in part by the desire to simplify the tax system which we admitted was complicated.
The way to tax simplification is not just a matter of simpler language. The way in which our tax is structured inevitably has a bearing on how complex or simple the tax law must be. At the same time we must recognize that, if we want to achieve certain policy goals in taxation, sometimes the inevitable result is some increased complexity in the tax law. For example, the Minister has announced his intention to introduce a minimum tax effective next year. The goal of this initiative has received widespread support. One result would be to make the tax system somewhat more involved. It will mean an addition to individual tax returns. That will be one cost of achieving an important step toward greater equity in our tax system. I think the extra effort will be worth it.

However, Mr. Speaker, this principle being put forward, this idea of a minimum tax, requires a package of very specific measures which would change the existing Income Tax Act which, God knows, already is complex enough. Before introducing this new measure haphazardly, it is very important that we give a general idea of what it is, based on the principles, to the entire community by way of a proposal tabled in Parliament, in order that we may benefit from all Canadian expertise, all the expertise in those special areas.

There have been two other recent developments that have improved our process of legislating tax changes. One is the practice begun by the Department of Finance of issuing technical notes to help explain how individual clauses in tax Bills before the House will work and how they fit into the Income Tax Act. Those notes are of great value, both to Members of this House and to taxpayers and their technical advisers who must work with the new laws which are constantly in evolution.
The other innovation begun this year involves income tax amendments that are of a technical nature not involving any new policy. By putting these together in a separate Bill, apart from the Budget measures, they can be brought forward for consideration quite apart from the Budget measures. This process helps to liberate the Budget from a welter of technical matters and improves the over-all Budget process.

It is true that formerly, having tried to read through the previous budget, it was quite a nuisance to have a collection of technical notes obscure our view of the basic principles that
November 1, 1985

were dictated in the previous budgets. In the last budget we wanted to set out principles first while encouraging people to be careful in their interpretation and to consult what was to follow-

In conclusion, I submit that the Government has taken a number of important steps toward improving our tax laws and the manner in which tax changes are legislated by this House. Further reforms are proposed in the Budget discussion paper of last May dealing with the budgetary process.
Further, I can assure the Hon. Member for Western Arctic that the Government is prepared to consider any more suggestions for improving that process.

Mr. Speaker, of course the House of Commons and the Canadian people should not be asked to trust their Government without question and to depend solely on the administration and interpretation of complex legislation by experts.
However, I think that we should all understand that the law is a complex thing which requires specialized interpretations that cannot be made only through policy statements.

I have just listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier). I felt like saying after he concluded his speech that he could make it again, but in plain language as the motion says.
I notice you, Mr. Speaker, even had difficulty at times understanding the technical remarks. I noticed that you were very deep in thought trying to understand completely what was being said.

speechtext:
Yes, he is a very good lawyer. The Speaker had extreme difficulty at times following the hon. gentleman's remarks.
The motion presented by the Member for Western Arctic is very well taken. If at all possible, the Government should aim at simplifying its laws and the way it carries out its regulations.
Because the statutes at times are rather complicated and complex in their wording, you have the communications that arise from that law to the people of Canada also complex and complicated in the written word. In other words, in most instances where a person has been found to be included or excluded from a particular program of the Government you see a constituent, a person, receiving a letter saying something like: "You are not eligible for this program because you contravened section such and such of such and such an Act". That is all the explanation given. I am thinking particularly
Ways and Means Motions
about the Unemployment Insurance Act and certain other matters that arise out of taxation legislation.
The point is well taken by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic. One need only look at the legislation presented in this Chamber recently by the Government to see exactly why the point being made by the gentleman from Western Arctic is well taken. A lot of definitions especially in recent legislation, especially since the Tory Government took over, are somewhat hazy, general and certainly not specific and certainly not in plain language as they should be.
We have been debating for the last few days in this House terms like workforce, designated groups and aboriginal peoples that are contained in legislation but certainly not described to people. We have listened to the Government of Canada announce programs that say: "We are going to try to assist those who are unemployed". We know that the definition of unemployed by the Government of Canada these days is quite different from the definition the ordinary person would assume would be attached to that word, that is, the dictionary explanation. We look back to what is "unemployed" under such and such an Act or the definition of a fisherman or a farmer under such and such an Act or statute. As the Hon. Member for Western Arctic has put it, it makes much more sense to introduce legislation to have statutes on the books that are in plain English so people can understand.
We all recognize that we would perhaps be putting some lawyers out of business and perhaps even some juges. Unfortunately a lot of the cases before the appeal courts today having to do with the Tax Court of Canada and about which we are talking indirectly here today are there because it is unclear to the Canadian involved just what the law is.
I support the hon. gentleman's resolution before the Chamber and I hope that the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Went-worth (Mr. Scott) will also be very brief so we can get on with this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it goes without saying that I will have to be brief since we have about four and one-half minutes left.
As my brief form of introduction, it is all very well to suggest that we should draft our income tax Bills and propose changes in plain simple unpretentious English and French in contrast to the unintelligible gobbledegook that has been devised under many years of Liberal rule, but the problem is that simple language or lack of precision means tax lawyers and other experts could drive trucks through the income tax system. While I know it is raw heresy to suggest that many wealthy tax lawyers probably earn their hefty remuneration by finding loopholes in the existing tax system by performing the most ingenious end runs around the laws as they stand now, surely the Government's task is to make the language in the tax system more easily understood to the average taxpayer. The hilarious example referred to by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) indicates the urgent need for that.

November !, 1985
Ways and Means Motions
With all due respect to my colleague from Western Arctic, we cannot and we must not hinder rather than help the goal of legislating better tax laws. Talking the language of Sesame Street might make the tax system a little more entertaining, if anything about taxes can be called entertaining, but Big Bird would only make things more confusing for Canadian taxpayers. I happen to prefer the language of "Big Mike", the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). In the Canadian Budgetary Process Proposals for Improvement, on page 13, there is a whole list of technical matters and proposals for improvement. That document was released May, 1985. It clearly indicates that the Government is moving toward the initiative, the very worth-while and laudable suggestion made by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), to simplify the language to make it plain. As I said, plain language while a laudable objective, is not the only answer to simplifying our tax system. Millions of Canadians and thousands of Canadian businesses depend on the precision of proposed tax laws in order to assess changes to their tax liability. A lack of precision, Mr. Speaker, creates greater uncertainty and that is not in my view in the interests of Canadian taxpayers. The inclusion of detailed Ways and Means motions promotes the consultation process between private Canadians and the Canadian Government. Detailed motions will allow specialists outside the Government to comment on the specific language that the Government intends to use.
Should the language prove not to accomplish the policy objectives of the Government, the language can now be changed. I certainly hope that one paragraph quoted by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap is put up as a prime example of some language that needs to be changed.
I suggest that it is the Hon. Member's intention to promote the importance of tax simplification, and for that reason it is a worth-while proposition, but his ways and means of doing it are not quite acceptable to the Government.
